title: Best Dehumidifier Air Conditioner Combos (2026): AC + Dry Mode
h1: The Best Dehumidifier Air Conditioners and AC Combos
dek: Every air conditioner wrings some water out of the air. These are the units — and the add-ons — that do it best.
description: The best dehumidifier air conditioner combos for 2026, plus whether ACs really dehumidify, how dry mode works and when an AC and dehumidifier belong together.
intro: Shopping for a **dehumidifier air conditioner** usually starts with a simple question: do air conditioners dehumidify at all? They do. Every AC cools by pulling warm room air across a cold coil, and when that coil is below the air's dew point, water condenses and drains away. The catch is that the moisture removal is a side effect. The thermostat, not the humidity, decides when the compressor runs, so on mild, sticky days your AC can switch off long before the room actually feels dry.

That's why the best combination for most homes is either an AC with a genuinely useful **dry mode** — ideally one with an inverter compressor that can run long, gentle cycles — or a good air conditioner paired with a dedicated dehumidifier for the shoulder seasons. Homes with central air have a third option: a whole-house dehumidifier that rides on the same ductwork.
Below are our picks across all three approaches, from window and portable ACs with dehumidify modes to the standalone and ducted dehumidifiers that make an air conditioner work better.
topPicksLead: For a single room, the **Midea Duo** is our top AC-and-dehumidifier combo, because its inverter compressor keeps drying the air instead of cycling off the moment the room hits temperature.

blocks.text: That first number is the heart of the matter. An air conditioner spends most of its effort lowering temperature. On hot days that's plenty of drying; on a 72°F rainy day, the AC hardly runs at all.

sections.heading: How we pick dehumidifier air conditioners

blocks.text: We don't run a test lab. For this guide we compared manufacturer specs and manuals for compressor type, dry or dehumidify modes and drainage, ENERGY STAR listings for efficiency, and the CPSC recall database. Then we read owner reviews for recurring complaints: rooms that stay clammy, leaking drain ports, noisy compressors.

We gave the most weight to inverter compressors, which can run long, low-speed cycles that dry the air instead of short-cycling, and to options that control humidity on their own setting. We left out single-hose portables, which pull humid outdoor air into the house while they run.

sections.heading: What to look for in an AC and dehumidifier combo

items.label: An inverter compressor
items.text: It slows down instead of switching off, so the coil stays cold and keeps condensing water. This matters more for humidity than raw BTUs.

items.label: A real dry mode
items.text: Look for a dedicated dry or dehumidify setting — the water-drop icon on the remote — not just a low fan speed.

items.label: The right size, not the biggest
items.text: An oversized AC cools the room in minutes and shuts off before it dries the air. Size by the room, not by the hottest day of the year.

items.label: Drainage you can live with
items.text: In dehumidify mode, a portable can collect real water. A drain port and hose save you from emptying a tray.
sub: Window units drip outside, which is one reason they're simpler.
Dedicated dehumidifiers can drain by gravity or a built-in pump.

items.label: A way to measure humidity
items.text: Most ACs don't display humidity. A cheap hygrometer tells you whether dry mode is actually working or whether you need a dedicated dehumidifier.

blocks.text: Yes, but only while the compressor is running and the coil is cold. When warm air passes over an evaporator coil below its dew point, water vapor condenses on the fins, drips into a pan and leaves through a condensate line — or, in a window unit, out the back.

The amount depends on how long the system runs. On a 95°F afternoon, long cycles wring out a lot of water. On a mild, humid day, the thermostat is satisfied within minutes, and the compressor stops long before the coil has done much drying. Our [dehumidifier vs. air conditioner](/guides/dehumidifier-vs-air-conditioner/) guide walks through which machine fixes which problem.
How an oversized AC unit fails to dehumidify

An AC that's too big for the space hits the thermostat setting too quickly. Short cycles mean the coil spends much of each run just getting cold, and the water it does collect may still be clinging to the fins when the compressor stops. If the blower keeps running, that water re-evaporates straight back into the house. The result is the classic cold-but-clammy room.

items: **Set the thermostat fan to Auto, not On**, so the blower doesn't blow moisture off a wet coil between cycles.
**Use a thermostat's dehumidify feature** if it has one; some slow the blower or let the AC cool slightly below setpoint to dry the air.
**Ask about variable-speed or two-stage equipment** when it's time to replace a system. They run longer at lower output, which is better for humidity.

sections.heading: Will a dehumidifier help my AC?

blocks.text: Usually, yes. Drier air feels cooler, so many households can raise the thermostat a degree or two once humidity is under control, and the AC spends less effort on moisture. A dehumidifier does give off a little warmth, though, so it won't cool a room on its own — more on that in [does a dehumidifier cool a room?](/guides/does-a-dehumidifier-cool-a-room/)

items: Let the air conditioner handle hot afternoons, when its long cycles dry the air too.
Set a dehumidifier to 45–50% for mild, rainy stretches when the AC barely runs.
Put the dehumidifier in the dampest area — often the basement — not next to an AC vent.
Once humidity is steady, nudge the thermostat up a degree and see if you notice the difference.

blocks.title: Running cost check
blocks.text: A 50-pint ENERGY STAR dehumidifier uses far less power than running central air just to dry the house. Our [electricity guide](/guides/how-much-electricity-does-a-dehumidifier-use/) has the math.

For a single room, the **Midea Duo** is the best AC and dehumidifier combo, and the **Midea U** is the window unit to get if your window allows it. With central air, add the **Aprilaire E100** to dry the whole house on its own schedule. And if your AC is fine but the house still feels damp, don't replace it — pair it with a dedicated dehumidifier like the **Midea Cube 50** and let each machine do the job it was built for.

faqs.a: Yes. Water condenses on the cold coil and drains away whenever the compressor runs. But removal depends on run time, so on mild, humid days when the AC cycles off quickly, it removes much less moisture than people expect.

faqs.q: Is there a window air conditioner with a dehumidifier built in?
faqs.a: Many window ACs include a dry or dehumidify mode, including the Midea U. It helps on muggy days, but it doesn't hold an exact humidity setting the way a standalone dehumidifier does.

faqs.q: What does dehum or dry mode on my AC do?
faqs.a: It runs the compressor with a slow fan so the coil stays colder and condenses more water, while cooling less aggressively. It's useful when the room is comfortable but sticky.

faqs.q: Dehumidifier vs. AC: which should I buy?
faqs.a: If the room is hot, buy an air conditioner. If it's comfortable but damp, especially a basement, buy a dehumidifier. Many humid-climate homes end up with both.

faqs.q: Will a dehumidifier help my AC?
faqs.a: Usually. Removing moisture takes load off the air conditioner and lets you set the thermostat a little higher. Just keep the dehumidifier away from the AC's return or vents so they don't work against each other.

faqs.q: Can you add a dehumidifier to a central air conditioner?
faqs.a: Yes. Whole-house dehumidifiers such as the Aprilaire E100 tie into existing ductwork and run on their own humidity control. Installation is usually a job for an HVAC contractor.

faqs.q: Does a portable AC unit dehumidify?
faqs.a: Yes, all portable ACs remove some moisture, and most have a dehumidify mode. Dual-hose and hose-in-hose designs handle humid weather better than single-hose units, which pull outside air into the house.
